For this reason the husband is obligated to suffer the prescribed punishment if he does not perform li'an, so beginning with him in li'an is more fitting than beginning with her.

[Section: Neither of them is accepted with fewer than five repetitions]

Among its features is that the man's li'an is not accepted with fewer than five repetitions, nor is the woman's. It is not accepted from him to substitute the curse with wrath, distancing or anger, nor from her to substitute wrath with curse, distancing or anger. Rather, each of them brings what Allah has prescribed for him or her of these, both in law and by decree. This is the more correct of the two opinions in the school of Ahmad, Malik and others.

Among its features is that it does not require adding anything to the wording mentioned in the Qur'an and the Sunnah. Indeed, it is not recommended to do so. He does not need to say: "I testify by Allah, besides whom there is no god, the Knower of the unseen and the seen, who knows the secret as He knows the open," or the like. Rather, it is sufficient for him to say: "I testify by Allah that I am truly among the truthful," and she says: "I testify by Allah that he is truly among the liars." He does not need to say: "concerning what I have accused her of, adultery," nor should she say: "he is truly among the liars concerning what he accused me of, adultery." It is not required that, if he claims to have seen it, he says: "I saw her committing adultery like the kohl stick in the kohl pot." There is no basis for this in the Book of Allah or the Sunnah of His Messenger. Allah, glorified is He, in His knowledge and wisdom, has sufficed us with what He has legislated for us and commanded us, without the burden of adding to it.

[Section heading]
Ibn Sa'd said: During this expedition (the expedition of al-Muraysi') Aisha's necklace fell, and the people halted to search for it, and the verse of tayammum (dry ablution) was revealed.

Al-Tabarani mentioned in his Mu'jam, from the hadith of Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Yahya ibn 'Abbad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, from his father, from Aisha, who said: "When the matter of my necklace happened, what happened happened, and the people of the slander said what they said. Then I went out with the Prophet ﷺ on another expedition, and my necklace also fell, until its search held the people back. I met from Abu Bakr what Allah willed, and he said to me: 'O little daughter, in every journey you are a burden and a trial, and there is no water with the people.' So Allah revealed the concession of tayammum." This indicates that the story of the necklace, for which tayammum was revealed, was after this expedition, which is the apparent view. But in that expedition the story of the slander occurred because of the loss and search of the necklace, so some people confused one of the two stories with the other. We will point out the story of the slander.

That is because Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, had been taken out by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with him on this expedition by a lot that fell upon her, and that was his custom with his wives. When they returned from the expedition, they stopped at some of the stations, and Aisha went out for her need, then returned, and she missed a necklace belonging to her sister which she had borrowed. She returned to search for it at the place where she had lost it. The men who used to carry her howdah came, and they thought she was in it, so they lifted the howdah, not noticing its lightness, because Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, was young and had not been covered by the flesh that would have made her heavy. Also, when the men cooperated in lifting the howdah, they did not notice its lightness; had the one who lifted it been one or two people, the state would not have been hidden from them. So Aisha returned to their stopping place, having found the necklace, and there was no caller nor any answerer. She sat in the place, thinking that they would miss her and return to look for her. Allah is overpowering over His affair; He manages the affair from above His Throne as He wills. So her eyes overcame her and she slept, and she did not wake except by the words of Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal: "Indeed we belong to Allah and to Him we return, the wife of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ!"

Safwan had stayed behind at the rear of the army, because he was a heavy sleeper, as came from him in Sahih Abi Hatim.

In the Sunan:
When he saw her, he recognized her, for he had seen her before the revelation of the hijab. He said the istirja', made his mount kneel, and brought it close to her. She mounted it, and he did not speak a single word to her, and she heard from him nothing but his istirja'. Then he led her on, guiding her, until he arrived with her, and the army had stopped at the height of midday. When the people saw that, each one spoke according to his own disposition and what befitted him. The wicked enemy of Allah, Ibn Ubayy, found an outlet, so he breathed out from the anguish of hypocrisy and envy that was between his ribs, and he began to elaborate the slander, to spread it, to broadcast it, to gather it and to divide it, and his companions drew near to him through it.

When they came to Medina, the people of the slander spread the talk widely, while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ remained silent and did not speak. Then he consulted his companions about separating from her. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, advised him to divorce her and take another, by allusion and not by explicit statement. Usama and others advised him to keep her and not to pay attention to the words of the enemies. 'Ali, seeing that what was said was doubtful, advised abandoning doubt and suspicion for certainty, so that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ might be freed from the worry and grief that had reached him from the people's talk. So he advised cutting off the disease. Usama, knowing the love of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for her and for her father, and knowing her chastity, innocence, protection and piety, which were beyond all that and greater than it, and knowing the honour of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with his Lord, his station with Him, and His defense of him, that He would not make the mistress of his house and his beloved among women, and the daughter of his true friend, to be in the position the people of the slander had placed her; and that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is more honoured by his Lord and more dear to Him than to have under him a adulterous woman. He knew that the truthful one (al-Siddiqah), the beloved of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, is more honoured by her Lord than that He would test her with immorality while she is under His Messenger. And whoever's knowledge of Allah and knowledge of His Messenger and his estimation of Allah's greatness is strong in his heart, says what Abu Ayyub and other leading Companions said when they heard that: "Glory be to You, this is a tremendous slander" [al-Nur: 16].

And reflect on what there is in their glorifying Allah and declaring Him free of imperfection in this position, of knowledge of Him, and of declaring Him far above what does not befit Him, that He would make for His Messenger, His intimate friend and the most honoured of creation before Him, a wicked adulterous woman. Whoever thinks of Him, glory be to Him, such a thought has thought an evil thought of Him. And the people of knowledge of Allah and His Messenger know that a wicked woman is fit only for a wicked man, as Allah the Exalted said: "Wicked women are for wicked men" [al-Nur: 26]. So they decided with a certainty about which they had no doubt that this was a tremendous slander and a manifest falsehood.

If it is said: Why then did the Messenger of Allah ﷺ hesitate about her affair, and ask about her, and investigate, and consult, while he is the most knowing of Allah, of his own station with Him, and of what befits Him? Why did he not say: "Glory be to You, this is a tremendous slander," as the excellent Companions said?

The answer: This is among the complete wisdoms which Allah made this story a cause for, and a test and trial for His Messenger ﷺ and for the entire Ummah until the Day of Resurrection, so that by this story He might raise some peoples and lower others, "and Allah increases those who are guided in guidance and faith, and He does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss" [cf. Muhammad: 17]. The completion of the test and trial required that revelation be withheld from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for a month concerning her affair, no revelation being sent to him about it, so that His wisdom which He had decreed and ordained might be completed and appear in the most perfect forms, and that the sincere believers might increase in faith and steadfastness upon justice, truthfulness, good opinion of Allah, His Messenger, the People of his House, and the truthful among His servants; and that the hypocrites might increase in falsehood and hypocrisy, and that He might manifest to His Messenger and the believers their inner secrets; and that the worship intended from the truthful one and her two parents might be completed, and His blessing upon them completed, and that their need, desire, and dependence, as well as their humility before Him, their good opinion of Him and their hope in Him, might be intensified, and that her hope in creatures might be cut off, and that she might despair of obtaining victory and relief at the hand of any created being. For this reason she fulfilled this station its due when her parents said to her: "Get up and go to him," for Allah had revealed her innocence, and she said: "By Allah, I will not get up to him, nor will I praise anyone but Allah; it is He who revealed my innocence."

Also, among the wisdom of withholding revelation for a month was that the matter was tested and made pure, and the hearts of the believers were greatly turned toward what Allah would reveal to His Messenger concerning it, and they longed for that to the utmost longing. So the revelation came at the moment when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his household, the Siddiq and his family and companions and the believers most needed it, and it arrived upon them like rain upon land most in need of it, so it had the greatest and most gracious effect on them, and they rejoiced in it with complete joy, and they obtained from it the utmost delight. Had Allah informed His Messenger of the true state of affairs from the very first moment and sent down revelation immediately about it, these wisdoms would have been lost, and many times their equivalent, indeed many multiples of them.

The manifestation by Allah of the station of His Messenger ﷺ and of the People of his House with Him: Also, Allah the Glorified desired to manifest the station of His Messenger and the People of his House with Him, and their honour before Him, and to remove His Messenger from this affair, and that He Himself would take on the defense and protection of him, and the refutation of his enemies and the condemnation and censure of them, by a matter in which he had no action and to which he was not attributed; rather He Himself would be the one who takes on that for His Messenger and the People of his House.

Also, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was himself the intended target of harm, and his wife was the one accused. It would not have been fitting for him to testify to her innocence while knowing or thinking, with a thought close to knowledge, of her innocence. He never thought ill of her, and far be it from him and far be it from her. For this reason, when he sought to be excused from the people of the slander, he said: "Who will excuse me regarding a man whose harm has reached me concerning my family? By Allah, I know nothing of my family but good, and they have mentioned a man of whom I know nothing but good, and he never entered upon my family except with me." So he had, among the indications that testify to the innocence of the truthful one, more than the believers had. But because of the perfection of his patience, steadfastness, gentleness, good opinion of his Lord and trust in Him, he fulfilled the station of patience, steadfastness and good opinion of Allah its due, until revelation came to him with what gladdened his eye, delighted his heart, magnified his station, and made manifest to his Ummah the care of his Lord for him and His attention to his affair.

When revelation came with her innocence, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered that those who had openly spoken the slander be given eighty lashes each. He did not flog the wicked Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, although he was the head of the people of the slander. It was said that this is because the hudud are an expiation and a lightening for those who receive them, and the wicked one is not fit for that, and Allah has promised him a great punishment in the Hereafter, so that suffices him in place of the hadd. It was also said: Rather, he used to seek out the talk, gather it, relate it, and bring it out in forms that were not attributed to him. It was also said: The hadd is established only by confession or by evidence, and he did not confess to the slander, nor did anyone testify against him; he was only mentioning it among his companions, and they did not testify against him, nor did he mention it among the believers.

It was also said: The hadd for slander is a right of a human being, which is not executed except upon the demand of its claimant; and if it is said it is a right of Allah, then the demand of the one slandered is still necessary, and Aisha did not demand it from Ibn Ubayy.

It was also said: Rather, he left his hadd for a benefit greater than its enforcement, just as he left killing him despite the clear manifestation of his hypocrisy and his speaking words that required his killing many times; and that benefit was the conciliation of his people and the avoidance of repelling them from Islam, for he was obeyed among them and was their chief. So the risk of stirring up strife through his hadd could not be ruled out, and perhaps he was left alone for all these reasons.

So Mistah ibn Uthathah and Hassan ibn Thabit and Hamnah bint Jahsh were flogged, and these were among the sincere believers, as a purification and expiation for them. Abd Allah ibn Ubayy was left alone, and so he is not among those people.

[Section: On the strength of the faith of Aisha]

Whoever reflects on the words of the truthful one, when her innocence was revealed, "Her parents said to her: Get up to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. She said: By Allah, I will not get up to him, nor will I praise anyone but Allah," will know her knowledge, the strength of her faith, her attributing the blessing to her Lord, her singling Him out for praise in that station, her devotion to tawhid, the strength of her resolve, and her confidence in the clearness of her innocence, and that she had not done anything that would require her to rise in the station of one who seeks reconciliation and asks for it. Her confidence in the love of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for her made her say what she said, as an endearment of the beloved toward his beloved, especially in such a station, which is the finest station of endearment. She placed it in its proper place. How dear she was to him when she said, "I praise none but Allah, for it is He who revealed my innocence." How steadfast and composed she was, and this is the dearest thing to her, and she has no patience without it. Her beloved's heart had been estranged from her for a month, then she met his contentment and turning toward her, yet she did not hasten to rise to him, nor to rejoice in his pleasure and nearness, despite her intense love for him. This is the utmost in steadfastness and strength.

[Seeking his ﷺ excuse from one who slandered his family]

The disagreement about who responded to his ﷺ request for an excuse regarding a man whose harm had reached him concerning the People of his House, and likewise about when the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq took place.

In this matter, when the Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Who will excuse me regarding a man whose harm to my family has reached me?", Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, brother of Banu 'Abd al-Ashhal, stood up and said, "I will excuse you from him, O Messenger of God." This has troubled many scholars, for no scholar disputes that Sa'd ibn Mu'adh died shortly after his judgment concerning Banu Qurayzah following the Battle of the Trench (al-Khandaq), and that this was in the fifth year [AH], according to the correct view. The hadith of the slander (hadith al-ifk) is beyond doubt related to this expedition (ghazwah) of Banu al-Mustaliq, which is the expedition of al-Muraysi'. The majority hold that it took place after the Battle of the Trench, in the sixth year. So the accounts of people differed in answering this difficulty.

Musa ibn 'Uqbah said: "The expedition of al-Muraysi' was in the fourth year, before the Trench." Al-Bukhari transmitted this from him.

Al-Waqidi said: "It was in the fifth year. Qurayzah and the Trench came after it." Qadi Isma'il ibn Ishaq said: "They differed on this, and the more appropriate view is that al-Muraysi' was before the Trench. On this basis there is no difficulty, but people have held otherwise." The hadith of the slander also indicates something contrary to this, because 'A'ishah said that the incident occurred after the veil (hijab) had been revealed, and the verse of the veil was revealed concerning Zaynab bint Jahsh, and Zaynab was then married to him (ﷺ). He (ﷺ) asked her about 'A'ishah, and she said, "I protect my hearing and my sight." 'A'ishah said: "She was the one who competed with me among the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ)."

The historians have mentioned that his marriage to Zaynab took place in Dhu al-Qa'dah of the fifth year. On this basis, the statement of Musa ibn 'Uqbah is not sound.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: "The expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq was in the sixth year, after the Trench." He mentioned in it the hadith of the slander, except that he said, on the authority of al-Zuhri, from 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utbah, from 'A'ishah, and then related the hadith. He said: "Then Usayd ibn al-Hudayr stood up and said, 'I will excuse you from him.' Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah responded to him," and he did not mention Sa'd ibn Mu'adh.

Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm said: "This is the correct account, about which there is no doubt, and the mention of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh is an error, because Sa'd ibn Mu'adh died without doubt right after the conquest of Banu Qurayzah, and that was at the end of Dhu al-Qa'dah of the fourth year. The expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq was in Sha'ban of the sixth year, one year and eight months after the death of Sa'd. The exchange between the two men mentioned was after the return from the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq, by more than fifty nights."

I say: The correct view is that the Trench was in the fifth year, as will come.

[What has occurred of error in the hadith of the slander]

Among what has occurred in the hadith of the slander is that in one of the chains of al-Bukhari, from Abu Wa'il, from Masruq, who said: "I asked Umm Ruman about the hadith of the slander, and she related it to me." Many have said: "This is a clear error, for Umm Ruman died during the lifetime of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) descended into her grave," and he said: "Whoever would delight to look at a woman of the dark-eyed maidens of Paradise (al-hur al-'in), let him look at this one."

They said: "Even if Masruq had come to Madinah during her lifetime and asked her, he would have met the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and heard from him, but Masruq came to Madinah only after the death of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." They said: "Masruq has narrated from Umm Ruman a hadith other than this, reporting it without a link (irsal), so some narrators assumed that he had heard from her, and so they took this hadith to be a direct hearing. They said: 'Perhaps Masruq said: "Umm Ruman was asked," but it was distorted for some people into "she asked," because some people write the hamzah with an alif in every case.'"

Others said: "All of this does not reject the sound report which al-Bukhari included in his Sahih. Ibrahim al-Harbi and others have said that Masruq asked her when he was fifteen years old, and he died at the age of seventy-eight, and Umm Ruman was the earliest one from whom he narrated." They said: "As for the hadith about her death during the lifetime of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his descending into her grave, it is a hadith that is not sound. It has two defects which prevent its soundness. The first is that it was narrated by 'Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an, and he is weak in hadith, whose narrations are not used as proof. The second is that he narrated it from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, on the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ), and al-Qasim did not live during the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). How then can this be preferred over a hadith whose chain is like the sun, which al-Bukhari narrated in his Sahih?"

Masruq says in it: "I asked Umm Ruman and she related to me," and this rules out that the wording could be "she was asked."

Abu Nu'aym said in the book Ma'rifat al-Sahabah: "It has been said that Umm Ruman died during the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)," and this is an error.

[Section: Is the slave girl who testified concerning 'A'ishah Barirah?]

Among what has occurred in the hadith of the slander is that in one of its chains, 'Ali said to the Prophet (ﷺ) when he consulted him: "Question the slave girl, and she will tell you the truth." So he called Barirah and asked her, and she said: "I know nothing about her except what the goldsmith knows about gold," or as she said. This has been regarded as problematic, for Barirah entered into a contract of manumission (kitabah) and was freed only a long time after this. And al-Abbas, the paternal uncle of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), was then in Madinah, but al-Abbas came to Madinah only after the conquest (al-Fath). For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him, when he had interceded with Barirah that she return to her husband and she refused: "O 'Abbas, do you not wonder at Mughith's hatred for Barirah and her love for him!"

In the story of the slander, Barirah was not with 'A'ishah. If what they mentioned is necessary, then the error lies in naming the slave girl Barirah, and 'Ali did not say to him, "Ask Barirah," but said, "Question the slave girl, and she will tell you the truth," so some narrators thought she was Barirah and named her as such. And even if it does not necessarily follow that Mughith's request concerning her continued until after the conquest, and that he did not despair of her, the difficulty is resolved. And God knows best.

Ibn al-Qayyim (Tafsir al-Qayyim)

He specified the women by the wording, since they were the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), and so he stated them explicitly by their particular case. This is more correct than the understanding of those who, out of ignorance of the apparent meaning, said: "The intended meaning of al-muhsanat is the chaste private parts (al-furuj al-muhsanat)." For this is not what the listener understands from this wording, nor from His saying: ﴿And give them their bridal payments in a fair manner, as chaste women, not fornicators﴾ [al-Nisa': 25],

nor from His saying: ﴿And the chaste women from among the women﴾ [al-Nisa': 24],

nor from His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who accuse chaste, unaware, believing women﴾ [al-Nur: 23].

Rather, this is from the customary usage of the Lawgiver (urf al-shari'), where He expresses a general meaning by a specific term. This is other than the category of analogy (qiyas).

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 24, verse 26:

It has been explained that the verse means: bad words are for bad people and good words are for good people. It has also been explained that it means: good women are for good men and bad women are for bad men. The verse encompasses all of this and more. So good words, good deeds and good women belong to their like among the good people, and bad words, bad deeds and bad women belong to their like among the bad people. Allah, glorified and exalted is He, made all that is good (bi-hadhafirihi, in its entirety) to be in Paradise, and made all that is bad (in its entirety) to be in the Fire. He therefore made the abodes three: a abode made exclusively for the good people, which is forbidden to anyone other than the good people, and which has gathered every good thing, and this is Paradise.

And an abode made exclusively for the bad and the bad people,

and none enters it except the bad people, and this is the Fire.

And an abode in which the good and the bad are mixed and blended together, and this is this abode of ours. For this reason, trial and tribulation occur because of this mixing and blending, and that is in accordance with divine wisdom. When the Day of the return of creation comes, Allah distinguishes the bad from the good: He places the good and its people in an abode apart, where no others mix with them, and He places the bad and its people in an abode apart, where no others mix with them. Thus the matter returns to two abodes only: Paradise, which is the abode of the good people, and the Fire, which is the abode of the bad people. Allah, exalted is He, brings into being from the deeds of both groups their reward and their punishment. He makes the good words, deeds and characters of these people the very essence of their bliss and pleasures, and brings into being for them from these the most perfect causes of delight and joy. He makes the bad words, deeds and characters of the others the very essence of their torment and pains, and brings into being for them from these the greatest causes of punishment and pain, with consummate wisdom and a dominant, overwhelming might, so that He may show His servants the perfection of His lordship, the perfection of His wisdom, knowledge, justice and mercy, and so that His enemies may know that they were the fabricators and the liars, not His noble, truthful messengers. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they swore by Allah their most emphatic oaths that Allah will not resurrect those who die. Yes, it is a promise binding upon Him, but most of the people do not know. [He will resurrect them] to make clear to them that wherein they differ, and that those who disbelieved may know that they were liars﴾ [an-Nahl: 38-39].

The point is that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, made for happiness and wretchedness signs by which they are known. The happy good person is fit only for what is good, comes only with what is good, issues only what is good, and is associated only with what is good. The wretched bad person is fit only for what is bad, comes only with what is bad, issues only what is bad, and is associated only with what is bad. The bad person's badness gushes forth from his heart upon his tongue and limbs, and the good person's goodness gushes forth from his heart upon his tongue and limbs. A person may have two substances in him, and whichever of them prevails over him, he belongs to its people. If Allah wills good for him, He purifies him of the bad substance before the meeting, so that he meets Him on the Day of Resurrection purified, and does not need to be purified by the Fire; He purifies him from it by what He enables him to do of sincere repentance, effacing good deeds, and expiating calamities, until he meets Allah with no sin upon him. And He withholds from the other the materials of purification, so he meets Him on the Day of Resurrection with a bad substance and a good substance. His wisdom, exalted is He, refuses that anyone should dwell beside Him in His abode with his impurities, so He admits him into the Fire as a purification, a refinement and a smelting for him. When the ingot of his faith is cleansed of its dross, he is then fit to dwell beside Him and to live with His good servants.

The duration of this kind of people's stay in the Fire depends on how quickly those impurities are removed from them and how slowly. The quickest of them to be cleansed and purified are the quickest to come out, and the slowest are the slowest to come out. ﴿A recompense in accordance [with their deeds]﴾ [an-Naba: 26] ﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat: 46].

Since the polytheist is of wicked origin and wicked essence, the Fire does not purify his wickedness; rather, if he came out of it he would return wicked as he was, like the dog that enters the sea and then comes out of it. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, forbade Paradise to the polytheist.

Since the believer who is good and makes himself good is free of impurities, the Fire is forbidden to him, for there is nothing in him that requires his purification by it. Glory be to Him whose wisdom dazzles minds and intellects, and whose creatures' natures and reasons testify that He is the Most Wise of judges and Lord of the worlds; there is no god but Him.

**[Chapter: On the Benefits of Lowering the Gaze]**

The glance is a poisoned arrow from the arrows of Iblis, and whoever lets his glances loose, his regrets will endure. In lowering the gaze there are several benefits:

First: It is obedience to the command of Allah, which is the ultimate happiness of the servant in this life and the next. The servant has nothing more beneficial in his worldly life and his afterlife than obeying His commands. No one is wretched in this world and the Hereafter except through neglecting His commands.

Second: It prevents the effect of the poisoned arrow, which may be his destruction, from reaching his heart.

Third: It bequeaths to the heart intimacy with Allah and gathered attention upon Him. Letting the gaze roam scatters and disperses the heart and distances it from Allah. Nothing is more harmful to the heart than letting the gaze roam, for it causes estrangement between the servant and his Lord.

Fourth: It strengthens the heart and gladdens it, just as letting the gaze roam weakens it and saddens it.

Fifth: It gives the heart light, just as letting it roam clothes the heart in darkness. For this reason Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the Verse of Light right after the command to lower the gaze. He said: ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts﴾ (An-Nur 24:30).

Then, right after that, He said: ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The likeness of His light is like a niche in which there is a lamp﴾ (An-Nur 24:35).

That is, the likeness of His light is in the heart of His believing servant who obeys His commands and avoids His prohibitions. When the heart is illuminated, the streams of goodness come to it from every direction, just as when it is darkened, the clouds of trial and evil gather over it from every place. Whatever innovation, misguidance, following of desire, turning away from guidance, neglect of the causes of happiness, or occupation with the causes of wretchedness you wish, it is the light within the heart that reveals all of this to him. When that light departs, its owner remains like a blind man groping in the depths of darkness.

Sixth: It bequeaths a true insight (firasah, perceptive discernment) by which one distinguishes truth from falsehood, and the truthful from the liar.

Shuja al-Kirmani used to say: "Whoever cultivates his outward self by following the Sunnah, and his inward self by constant vigilance (muraqabah), and lowers his gaze from what is forbidden, restrains himself from doubtful matters, and nourishes himself with what is lawful, his insight will not err." And Shuja was a man whose insight never erred.

Allah, glorified is He, rewards the servant for his deed with something of the same kind. Whoever leaves something for Allah, Allah compensates him with something better. So when he lowers his gaze from what Allah has forbidden, Allah compensates him by letting loose the light of his inner vision, in exchange for restraining his sight for Allah's sake, and opens for him the door of knowledge, faith, recognition, and true insight, which is only attained through clear sight. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿By your life, they were wandering blindly in their intoxication﴾ (Al-Hijr 15:72).

He described them with intoxication, which is the corruption of the mind, and with blindness, which is the corruption of insight. So attachment to forms causes the corruption of the mind, the blindness of insight, and the intoxication of the heart, as the poet said:

*Intoxicated with the intoxication of desire, and with the intoxication of wine, *
*And when will the one who is drunk on it come to his senses?*

Another said:

*They said: "You have gone mad over the one you love," so I said to them: *
*Love is greater than what afflicts the madmen.*
*Love's owner never awakens for all time, *
*Rather, the madman is struck down in an instant.*

Seventh: It bequeaths to the heart steadfastness, courage, and strength. Allah combines for him the authority of victory and proof, and the authority of power and might. As in the report: "The one who opposes his desire, Satan flees from his shadow."

The opposite of this is what you find in one who follows his desire: the humiliation, lowliness, degradation, baseness, and contemptibility of the soul, which Allah places upon whoever disobeys Him. As al-Hasan said: "Even though mules trot with them and fine horses amble with them, the humiliation of disobedience is around their necks. Allah refuses except to humiliate whoever disobeys Him."

Allah, glorified is He, has made honor accompany obedience to Him and humiliation accompany disobedience to Him. He, Exalted, said: ﴿But honor belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ (Al-Munafiqun 63:8).

He, Exalted, also said: ﴿Do not weaken, nor grieve, for you will be superior if you are believers﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:139).

Faith is speech and action, outward and inward. He, Exalted, said: ﴿Whoever desires honor, then all honor belongs to Allah. To Him ascends the good word, and righteous deeds elevate it﴾ (Fatir 35:10).

That is, whoever desires honor should seek it through obedience to Allah and His remembrance, through the good word and righteous deed.

In the supplication of qunut (the supplication in the prayer): "Indeed, the one You befriend is never humiliated, and the one You oppose is never honored." Whoever obeys Allah has befriended Him in what he obeys Him in, and he has honor in proportion to his obedience. Whoever disobeys Him has opposed Him in what he disobeys Him in, and he has humiliation in proportion to his disobedience.

Eighth: It opens the door for Satan to enter the heart. He enters with the glance and penetrates the heart along with it, faster than air passes through an empty space. He then presents to him the image of the one looked at and adorns it, makes it an idol to which the heart devotes itself, then promises and deceives him, and kindles the fire of desire in the heart, throwing upon it the fuel of sins that could not have been reached without that image. Thus the heart is in flames.

From that blaze come those breaths in which he feels the heat of the fire, those sighs and burnings. The heart is surrounded by fires on every side, so it is in their midst like a sheep in the midst of an oven. For this reason, the punishment of those who pursue the desires of forbidden images is that a furnace of fire is prepared for them in the barzakh (the intermediate realm), and their spirits are placed in it until the Day their bodies are resurrected, as the Prophet (ﷺ) was shown it in a dream, in the hadith agreed upon as authentic.

Ninth: It empties the heart for reflection on its own interests and occupation with them. Letting the gaze roam makes one forget this and prevents him from it, so his affairs fall into disorder, he falls into following his desire, and into heedlessness of the remembrance of his Lord. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who follows his desire, and whose affair is excess﴾ (Al-Kahf 18:28).

Letting the gaze roam necessitates these three matters in proportion to its extent.

Tenth: Between the eye and the heart there is a passage and a path, such that each one moves the other and each is corrected by the other's correction and corrupted by the other's corruption. When the heart is corrupted, the gaze is corrupted; when the gaze is corrupted, the heart is corrupted. And likewise on the side of righteousness: when the eye is ruined and corrupted, the heart is ruined and corrupted, becoming like a garbage heap, a place of filth, refuse, and dirt. It is then unfit to house the knowledge of Allah, His love, turning to Him, intimacy with Him, and joy in His nearness. Only the opposites of these dwell in it.

**[Chapter: On Recounting a Debate Between the Heart and the Eye, Each Blaming the Other, and the Judgment Between Them]**

When the eye was the scout and the heart the driver and seeker, the eye enjoying the pleasure of seeing and the heart enjoying the thrill of conquest, they were partners in the reins of desire. But when they fell into hardship and shared the affliction, each began to blame and reproach the other.

The heart said to the eye: "You are the one who drove me to the watering places of destruction, and cast me into regrets by following your glances. You took your gaze on a stroll through those gardens, and sought cure from diseased eyelids. You opposed the word of the Wisest of the wise: ﴿Say to the believing men﴾ (An-Nur 24:30),

and the words of His Messenger: 'Looking at a woman is a poisoned arrow from the arrows of Iblis. Whoever abandons it out of fear of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, Allah will reward him with faith whose sweetness he will find in his heart.' Narrated by Imam Ahmad: Hushaym told us, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ishaq told us, from Mihareb ibn Dithar, from Silah, from Hudhayfah."

And 'Umar ibn Shabbah said: Ahmad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Yunus told us, 'Anbasa ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Qurashi told us, Abu al-Hasan al-Madani told us, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) told us, saying: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man's glance at a woman's beauty is a poisoned arrow from the arrows of Iblis. Whoever turns away from that arrow, Allah will bring him an act of worship that will gladden him."

So who is to blame, other than the one who shot his companion with the poisoned arrow? Do you not know that nothing is more harmful to a person than the eye and the tongue? Many have perished only through them, and more have been destroyed only because of them. How many a place of destruction have they led you to, and how many a fate of ruin have they brought you to! Whoever wishes to live happily or to live praiseworthy should restrain the reins of his gaze and his tongue, to be safe from harm, for harm lurks in excessive speech and excessive looking. The Truthful and Believed One (ﷺ) has clearly stated that the two eyes commit adultery, and they are the root of the adultery of the private parts, for they are its scouts and they call to it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about a sudden glance, and he commanded the questioner to turn his gaze away, guiding him to what would benefit him and ward off his harm. He also said to his cousin 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), warning him against what leads to temptation and brings regret: "Do not follow a glance with another glance." Have you not heard the words of the wise: whoever lets his gaze wander tires his thoughts; whoever has many glances has lasting regrets, his times are lost, and his tears flow. And the words of the poet:

*The glances of eyes toward eyes are what *
*made destruction a path to the heart.*
*The glances kept invading its heart *
*until it writhed in them as a slain one.*

Another said:

*You enjoyed a glance, O my eyes, *
*and you brought my heart to the watering places of destruction.*
*O my eyes, withdraw from my heart, for it *
*is the injustice of two who strove to kill one.*

**[Section]**

The eye said: "You wronged me first and last, and I bore the burden of your sin, inwardly and outwardly. I am only your messenger calling you to Him and your scout guiding you to Him.

*When you send a scout toward the one you love *
*and then blame him, you have wronged the scout.*

You are the king who is obeyed, and we are the soldiers and followers. You mounted me on the post-horses for your need, then you turned upon me with threats and warnings. If you had commanded me to close my door and lower my curtain, I would have heard and obeyed, and I would not have grazed in the protected pasture. You sent me to hunt prey whose snares and nets you had set and whose traps surrounded you. So I became a captive after being a commander, and a slave after being a king. Moreover, the Master of mankind and the most just of judges has ruled in my favor against you, when he said: 'Indeed, in the body there is a morsel of flesh; when it is sound, the whole body is sound, and when it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Truly, it is the heart.' Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) said: 'The heart is the king, and the limbs are its soldiers. If the king is good, his soldiers are good, and if the king is wicked, his soldiers are wicked.' If you had reflected well, you would have known that the corruption of your subjects is due to your corruption, and their rectitude and guidance is due to your rectitude. But you were destroyed and you destroyed your subjects, and you placed your sin upon the weak eye, while the root of your affliction is that the love of Allah, the remembrance of Him, His speech, His names, and His attributes have departed from you. You turned toward other than Him, turned away from Him, and substituted the love of others, and desire for them, in place of Him.

Moreover, you have heard what was recounted about His denunciation, glorified is He, of the Children of Israel for exchanging one food for an inferior one, when He rebuked them for it, saying: ﴿Would you exchange that which is lower for that which is better?﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:61).

So how about one who exchanges the love of his Creator, Originator, Friend, and Owner of his affairs, in whom there is no goodness, success, bliss, joy, delight, or salvation, except by singling Him out in love and making Him dearer to him than all else! So consider, by Allah, for whom you have exchanged, and in exchange for the love of whom you have settled. Are you content for yourself to be imprisoned in a latrine while the hearts of those who love Him circle around the Throne? If you turned toward Him and away from all else, you would see wonders, and you would be safe from ruin and perdition. Do you not know that He specially grants success and bliss to whoever comes to Him with a sound heart, sound from all else, with nothing in it but His love and the pursuit of His pleasure?"

The eye said: "Between my sin and yours, in the eyes of people, is like the difference between my blindness and yours in analogy." And He in whose hand are the reins of all affairs has said: ﴿For indeed, it is not the eyes that are blind, but it is the hearts within the breasts that are blind﴾ (Al-Hajj 22:46).

**[Section]**

When the liver heard their dialogue and their dispute took hold, it said: "You two have helped each other toward my destruction, and cooperated to kill me. How justly has the one who recounted your debate spoken, complaining on my behalf against you both. He says:

*My eyelid stirred for my heart a sickness, *
*while the eye claims that the heart hurt it.*
*The body testifies that the eye is lying, *
*for it is the one that stirred the heart's affliction.*
*Were it not for the eyes and what they reap of sickness, *
*I would not have been cast down among their slain.*

Then the wronged liver said: 'Be patient! You have cut me off, and you did not fear Allah.'"

Another said:

*My heart says to my eye when it weeps in anguish: *
*"You weep, yet you are the one who burdened me with pain."*
*My eye replied to it in what it reproached it for: *
*"Rather, you are the one who burdened me with hopes and longing."*
*Until, when each was alone with its companion, *
*both were content with long illness.*
*My liver called to them: "Do not be far away, for you *
*have cut me off, with what you have met, a cutting."*

Another said:

*I reproached my heart when I saw my body wasted, *
*so it blamed my eye and said: "You were the messenger."*
*My eye said to my heart: "Rather, you were the guide."*
*I said: "Both of you, stop! You have left me slain."*

Then she said: "I will take on the judgment between you both. You two are partners in the reins of affliction, just as you are two steeds in a race of pleasure and delight. The eye enjoys, while the heart longs and desires. For this reason, the one who said it about you both said:

*When I had forgotten love, my gaze *
*gave my heart a reminder, so my heart said to me: "You too have joy."*
*You freed yourself from the vigil of your nights awake, *
*and freed me from the anguish of separation and sickness.*
*We both rejoice in the endurance of love, but if you *
*were to last, neither you nor I would be preserved by passion.*"

If the grace of the Turner of hearts and eyes does not reach you both, then you have no comfort, and the heart has no rest. The poet said:

*By Allah, I do not know whom to blame, *
*for love: my soul, my accursed eye, or my heart.*
*If I blame my heart, it says to me: "The eye saw." *
*And if I blame my eye, it says: "The sin is the heart's."*
*My eye and my heart have divided my blood between them, *
*so O Lord, be a help against the eye and the heart.*

She said this. When you gave the heart the water of love in your cups, you kindled upon it the fire of longing. Vapor rose up toward you, and it dripped from you. So you choked on its drink at first, and you choked on the sea of its fire second. He said:

*Take my hand, then uncover the garment and look: *
*the wasting of my body, though I conceal it.*
*What flows from the eye is not its water, *
*but a spirit melting and dripping away.*

She said: "And the judge between you two is the One who judges between the spirit and the body when they dispute before Him. In the well-known report: the dispute among the creatures will not cease on the Day of Resurrection until the spirit and the body dispute. The body says to the spirit: 'You are the one who moved me, commanded me and directed me; otherwise I would not have moved or acted without you.' The spirit says to it: 'You are the one who ate, drank, indulged and enjoyed yourself, so you are the one who deserves punishment.' Then Allah, glorified is He, sends to them an angel to judge between them. He says: 'Your example is that of a paralyzed man who can see and a blind man who can walk. The two entered a garden. The paralyzed man said to the blind man: "I can see the fruits in it, but I cannot stand up." The blind man said: "I can stand up, but I cannot see anything." The paralyzed man said to him: "Come, carry me, for you walk and I reach the fruit." So upon which of them will the punishment fall?' He says: 'It falls upon both of them.' He said: 'So it is with you two.'"

And with Allah is success.

(Section)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts. That is purer for them. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what they do.﴾

He made purity (zakah) come after lowering the gaze and guarding the private parts.

For this reason, lowering the gaze from what is forbidden brings three great benefits of immense importance and high rank:

The first: the sweetness and pleasure of faith, which is sweeter, more delightful and more pleasant than what one turns one's gaze away from and leaves for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. Whoever leaves something for Allah, Allah replaces it for him with something better. The soul is inclined to love looking at beautiful forms, and the eye is the scout of the heart. So it sends its scout to look at what is there. When the scout informs it of the beauty and loveliness of what is looked at, the heart is stirred with longing for it. Often the scout tires and exhausts both the heart and its messenger, as it has been said:

"Whenever you send your glance as a scout for your heart, one day the sights will exhaust you.
You see what you cannot entirely possess, nor can you be patient over part of it."

When the scout refrains from uncovering and gazing, the heart rests from the burden of seeking and desire. Whoever lets his glances loose, his regrets endure, for looking generates love. Then a relationship begins in which the heart becomes attached to the one looked at. Then it grows stronger and becomes ṣabābah (infatuated longing), when the heart inclines toward it with its whole being.

Then it grows stronger and becomes gharām (passionate attachment) that clings to the heart, like a creditor who never leaves his debtor. Then it grows stronger and becomes ʿishq (passionate love), which is excessive love.

Then it grows stronger and becomes shaghaf (deep love), which is love that has reached the shaghāf (inner covering) of the heart and penetrated it. Then it grows stronger and becomes tatayyum.

Tatayyum is servitude, and from it comes "tayyamahu al-ḥubb" when love enslaves him. "Taym Allah" means the servant of Allah. So the heart becomes a slave to one who is not fit for it to be a slave to.

All of this is the offense of the look. At that point the heart falls into captivity. It becomes a prisoner after it was free, and confined after it was unrestricted. It complains of the glance and grieves over it, and the glance says: "I am your scout and your messenger, and you sent me."

This befalls only those hearts that are empty of love for Allah and sincerity toward Him, for the heart must attach itself to something beloved. Whoever does not have Allah alone as his beloved, his god and his object of worship, his heart will inevitably be bound to something else.

Allah, exalted is He, said about Yusuf the Truthful, peace be upon him: ﴿Thus, that We might turn away from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was of Our chosen, sincere servants.﴾ [Yusuf: 24]

So the wife of the ʿAzīz, being a polytheist, fell into what she fell into, despite being a married woman. Yusuf, peace be upon him, because he was sincere to Allah, was saved from that, despite being a young, unmarried, foreign slave.

The second benefit of lowering the gaze: the light of the heart and soundness of firasah (insight). Abu Shuja' al-Kirmani said: "Whoever adorns his outward with following the Sunnah, his inward with constant vigilance, restrains his soul from desires, lowers his gaze from what is forbidden, and is accustomed to eating what is lawful, his firasah will never err." Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the story of the people of Lot and what they were afflicted with, then said afterward: ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for those who discern.﴾ [al-Hijr: 75]

They are the ones with firasah who were spared from forbidden looking and immorality. Allah, exalted is He, also said right after His command to the believers to lower their gaze and guard their private parts: ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth.﴾ [al-Nur: 35]

The secret of this statement is that reward is of the same kind as the deed. Whoever lowers his gaze from what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has forbidden him, Allah compensates him with something of the same kind that is better. Just as he withheld the light of his sight from what is forbidden, Allah releases the light of his insight and heart, so he sees with it what one who let his gaze loose and did not lower it from the prohibitions of Allah does not see. This is something a person perceives in himself. The heart is like a mirror, and desire is like rust upon it. When the mirror is cleared of rust, the forms of realities are imprinted upon it as they truly are. When it is rusted, the forms of knowledge are not imprinted upon it. Then his knowledge and speech become mere conjecture and guesswork.

The third benefit: the strength, steadfastness and courage of the heart. Allah gives him, through his strength, the authority of victory, just as He gave him, through His light, the authority of proof. So He combines the two authorities for him, and Satan flees from him, as in the report: "Whoever opposes his desire, Satan flees from his shadow."

For this reason, in the one who follows his desire there is found the humiliation, weakness and abasement of the soul that Allah has placed upon those who disobey Him. He, glorified is He, made honor belong to those who obey Him and humiliation to those who disobey Him. Allah said: ﴿Honor belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers.﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]

And He said: ﴿Do not be weak and do not grieve, and you will be superior if you are believers.﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 139]

And He said: ﴿Whoever desires honor—then to Allah belongs all honor.﴾ [Fatir: 10]

That is, whoever seeks honor should seek it through obedience to Allah: through good speech and righteous deeds.

Some of the salaf said: "People seek honor at the doors of kings, and they do not find it except in obedience to Allah."

Al-Hasan said: "Even if the horses prance with them and the mules trot with them, the humiliation of disobedience is in their hearts. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, refuses except to humiliate whoever disobeys Him, for whoever obeys Allah, Exalted is He, has taken Him as his ally, and whoever Allah has as an ally is not humiliated," as in the supplication of qunut (the prayer supplication): "Indeed, the one whom You befriend is never humiliated, and the one whom You oppose is never honored."

The point is that the purification of the heart depends on its cleanliness, just as the purification of the body depends on purging it of its corrupt, bad humors. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy, not one of you would ever have been purified. But Allah purifies whom He wills, and Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾ [al-Nur: 21]

He mentioned this after the prohibition of adultery, slander, and marrying an adulteress, which indicates that purification is by avoiding these things.

Likewise is His saying, exalted is He, regarding seeking permission to enter homes: ﴿And if you are told, "Go back," then go back; it is purer for you.﴾ [al-Nur: 28]

For when they are commanded to return, lest they see a private matter which the homeowner would not like to be seen, that is purer for them, just as turning away and lowering the gaze is purer for the one who does it. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself and remembers the name of his Lord and prays.﴾ [al-Ala: 14–15]

And Allah, exalted is He, said about Musa, peace be upon him, in his address to Pharaoh: ﴿Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 18]

(Section: On the rulings regarding looking, its dangers, and what it inflicts upon its owner)

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts. That is purer for them. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what they do. And say to the believing women that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts...﴾ and the rest of the verse.

Since lowering the gaze is the foundation for guarding the private parts, He began by mentioning it. And since its prohibition is a prohibition of means (wasa'il), it is permitted for a stronger benefit, and forbidden if it is feared to lead to corruption and no greater benefit outweighs that corruption.

He, glorified is He, did not command lowering the gaze absolutely; rather, He commanded lowering "from" the gaze (min abṣārihim).

As for guarding the private parts, it is obligatory in every case and is not permitted except by its right. Therefore, the command to guard them is general.

Allah, glorified is He, made the eye the mirror of the heart. When the servant lowers his gaze, the heart lowers its desire and will; and when he lets his gaze loose, the heart lets its desire loose.

In the Sahih it is reported that al-Fadl ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, was riding behind the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the day of sacrifice, from Muzdalifah to Mina. Some women passed by on camels, and al-Fadl began to look at them. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ turned his head to the other side.

This is a prohibition and disapproval by action. Had looking been permissible, he would have approved it.

Also in the Sahih, from him (ﷺ), he said: "Indeed, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has prescribed for the son of Adam his share of adultery, which he will inevitably encounter. The eye commits adultery, and its adultery is looking. The tongue commits adultery, and its adultery is speech. The foot commits adultery, and its adultery is walking. The hand commits adultery, and its adultery is seizing. The heart desires and wishes, and the private part either confirms that or denies it." He began with the adultery of the eye because it is the root of the adultery of the hand, the foot and the heart, and the private part. He drew attention to the adultery of the tongue through speech, which leads to the adultery of the mouth through kissing. He made the private part confirm this if the act is carried out, or deny it if it is not. This hadith is among the clearest evidence that the eye disobeys by looking, and that this is its adultery. Therefore it refutes those who permit looking absolutely.

It is also established that he said: "O ʿAli, do not follow a glance with another glance, for the first is yours, but the second is not yours."

A question arose: "What do the scholars say about a man who looked at a woman once, and her love became attached to his heart, and the matter grew hard upon him. His soul said to him: 'All of this is from the first glance. If you looked at her again, you would see that she is less than what is in your soul, and you would be cured of her.' Is it permissible for him to deliberately look a second time for this purpose?"

The answer: Praise be to Allah, this is not permissible, for ten reasons:

First: Allah, glorified is He, commanded lowering the gaze, and did not make the cure for the heart lie in what He has forbidden to the servant.

Second: The Prophet ﷺ was asked about the sudden glance, and he knew that it affects the heart, yet he commanded treating it by turning away the gaze, not by repeating the look.

Third: He declared that the first look is for you, but the second is not for you. It is impossible that his illness should come from what is his, while its cure lies in what is not his.

Fourth: Evidence shows that the command to look once (the first glance) is stronger, and that a second look does not diminish it. Experience also testifies to this. The matter is as he saw it the first time, so it is not wise to risk repeating it.

Fifth: He may see something above what is in his soul, and so his torment increases.

Sixth: When Iblis intends a second glance, he stands at his mounts and adorns for him what is not good, so that the trial may be completed.

Seventh: He will not be aided in his affliction if he turns away from obeying the commands of the Sharia and seeks cure through what He has forbidden him. Rather, he is deserving that aid be withheld from him.

Eighth: The first glance is a poisoned arrow from the arrows of Iblis, and it is known that the second is more poisonous. So how can one cure poison with poison?

Ninth: The one in this situation is in the station of dealing with the Truth, Mighty and Majestic, by abandoning what he loves, as he claims. Yet he wants, through the second glance, to clarify the state of the one looked at. If she is not pleasing, he will leave her. So then his leaving her is because she does not suit his aim, not for Allah. Where then is dealing with Allah, glorified is He, by abandoning the beloved for His sake?

Tenth: It becomes clear through a matching example: if you ride a new horse and it inclines you toward a narrow path that has no exit and in which it cannot turn around to come out, then when it starts to enter, restrain it so that it does not enter. If it has entered a step or two, shout at it and turn it back quickly, before it can fully enter. If you turn it back, the matter is easy. But if you delay until it has entered and you have driven it inside, then you turn around to pull it by its tail, it becomes difficult for you, or its exit becomes impossible. Would any intelligent person say that the way to save it is to drive it further inside? So it is with the glance: when it affects the heart, if the prudent person hurries and cuts off the source from the beginning, its treatment is easy. But if he repeats the look, searches out the beauties of the image and transfers it to an empty heart, impressing it there, love becomes firmly established. And as the glances follow one another, they are like water given to a tree, and the tree of love never ceases to grow until the heart is corrupted, turns away from thought about what it was commanded, and its owner goes out to tribulations, committing forbidden acts and trials, and the heart is cast into ruin. The reason for this is that the one who looks has his eye delighted by the first glance, so it seeks a return, like eating a delicious food when one takes a morsel of it. Had he lowered his gaze at first, his heart would have rested and been safe.

Consider the words of the Prophet ﷺ: "The glance is a poisoned arrow from the arrows of Iblis." For the nature of the arrow is that it penetrates the heart and works in it as the poison works in the one who is poisoned. If he hastens to expel it, he is saved; otherwise it will certainly kill him.

Al-Marwadhi said: "I asked Ahmad about a man who looks at a female slave." He said: "I fear for him the trial. How many a glance has cast calamities into the heart of its owner!"

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Satan comes to a man through three things: his gaze, his heart and his remembrance. And he comes to a woman through three things: her gaze, her heart and her weakness."

Section: Since looking is among the closest means to what is forbidden, the Sharia required its prohibition and permitted it in cases of need. This is the case with every thing prohibited as a means, for it is permitted for a stronger benefit. Just as prayer is prohibited at the times of prohibition, lest it become a means of imitating the disbelievers in their prostration to the sun, so it is permitted for a stronger benefit, such as making up missed prayers, the funeral prayer, and prayers with causes, according to the correct view.

In the Musnad of Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, from the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "The glance is a poisoned arrow from the arrows of Iblis. Whoever lowers his gaze from the beauty of a woman, Allah will give his heart a sweetness that he will find until the day he meets Him." Or as he said.

Jarir ibn ʿAbd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the sudden glance, and he commanded me to turn my gaze away."

The sudden glance is the first look that occurs without the intention of the looker. As long as the heart does not intend it, one is not held accountable for it. But if he looks a second time deliberately, he sins. The Prophet ﷺ commanded whoever has a sudden glance to turn his gaze away and not continue looking, for prolonging it is like repeating it. He also guided one afflicted with a sudden glance to treat it by going to his wife, and said: "With her is like what is with her." For in that is consolation for the desired thing through its own kind.

Secondly, looking stirs the strength of desire, so he commanded him to diminish it by going to his family. So the trial of looking is the root of every trial, as is established in the two Sahihs from the hadith of Usama ibn Zayd, may Allah be pleased with them, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "I have left no trial after me more harmful to men than women."

In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Beware of the world, and beware of women."

In the Musnad of Muhammad ibn Ishaq al-Sarraj, from the hadith of ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ: "What I fear most for my nation are women and wine."

Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "None of the previous generations who disbelieved disbelieved except because of women, and those who remain disbelieve because of women."

[Section: The ruling on looking at a free woman and at a female slave]

As for the prohibition of looking at an elderly free woman who is ugly and repulsive, and its permissibility toward a female slave who is exceptionally beautiful, this is a lie against the Lawgiver. Where did Allah prohibit this and permit that?

Allah, glorified is He, only said: ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze﴾ [al-Nur: 30]

Allah and His Messenger did not permit the eyes to look at female slaves of exceptional beauty. And if one fears trial from looking at a female slave, it is undoubtedly forbidden for him. The confusion arose only because the Lawgiver prescribed for free women that they cover their faces from strangers, but did not require this of female slaves. However, this applies to female slaves engaged in service and daily work. As for concubines (umm walad and slave-concubines) who are customarily kept protected and veiled, where did Allah and His Messenger permit them to uncover their faces in markets, roads and gatherings of people, and permit men to enjoy looking at them?

This is a complete error against the Sharia. The mistake was reinforced by the fact that some jurists heard them say: "All of a free woman is 'awrah (the parts that must be covered) except her face and palms, and the 'awrah of a slave woman is what does not normally show, such as the stomach, back and shins." So he assumed that what normally shows has the same ruling as a man's face. This applies only to prayer, not to looking. The 'awrah is of two kinds: the 'awrah in looking and the 'awrah in prayer. A free woman may pray with her face and palms uncovered, but she may not go out in markets and gatherings of people in that state. And Allah knows best.

[Chapter: The Gaze is the Gateway to Sins]

Most sins enter upon a servant through these four doors, so we will mention in each door a section fitting for it.

**The Gaze**

As for glances, they are the forerunner of desire and its messenger. Guarding them is the root of guarding the private parts. Whoever lets his gaze roam casts himself into the places of destruction.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do not follow a glance with another glance, for the first is yours but the second is not yours."

In the Musnad (*al-Musnad*, the collection of Imam Ahmad) it is narrated from him (ﷺ):

"The glance is a poisoned arrow from the arrows of Iblis. Whoever lowers his gaze from the beauty of a woman for the sake of Allah, Allah will cause his heart to taste sweetness until the day he meets Him."

This is the meaning of the hadith.

He (ﷺ) also said: "Lower your gazes and guard your private parts."

And he (ﷺ) said: "Beware of sitting on the roadsides." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, our gatherings are something we cannot do without." He said: "If you must do so, then give the road its due." They said: "And what is its due?" He said: "Lowering the gaze, refraining from harm, and returning greetings."

The gaze is the root of most of the incidents that befall a person. A glance produces a passing thought; the passing thought produces an idea; the idea produces desire; desire produces intention; and it strengthens until it becomes a firm resolve, and then the act necessarily occurs, unless some preventer stops it.

For this it has been said: "Patience in lowering the gaze is easier than the patience through the pain that follows it."

The poet said:

*Every calamity begins with a glance,*
*and most of a great fire comes from a tiny spark.*

*How many a glance has reached the heart of its owner,*
*as far as an arrow reaches between the bow and its string.*

*The servant, as long as he has an eye that roams,*
*among the eyes of the beautiful is held hostage to danger.*

*It delights his eye but harms his soul;*
*no welcome to a joy that returns as harm.*

Among the harms of the gaze is that it produces sighs, sorrows and burnings. The servant sees what he is neither able to have nor able to bear to be without. This is among the greatest torments: that you see what you cannot bear to be without a part of, and cannot have a part of.

The poet said:

*Whenever you send your glance out as a scout*
*for your heart one day, the sights will exhaust you.*

*You see what you are neither able to possess entirely*
*nor able to endure being without some of it.*

This verse needs explanation. Its meaning is: you see what you cannot endure being without some of, and cannot have. His words "*you are not able to have all of it*" negate your ability over the whole, which cannot be negated except by negating the ability over each single part.

How many have sent out their glances, and they did not cease until he was writhing among them as a slain man, as it has been said:

*O you who look, whose glances have not stopped*
*until he thrashed among them, slain.*

And from my own verses:

*He grew weary of safety, so his glances became*
*devoted to a ruin he thinks is beautiful.*

*He kept following his glances, one after another,*
*until he thrashed among them, slain.*

A wonder: the glance of the looker is an arrow that does not reach the one looked at until it settles a place in the heart of the looker. From my own poem:

*O you who shoot with the arrows of glances, striving,*
*you are the one slain by what you shoot, so do not hit.*

*O you who sends the eye seeking its cure,*
*hold back your messenger lest it bring you ruin.*

What is more astonishing is that the glance wounds the heart with a wound, and it is followed by wound upon wound, yet the pain of the wound does not prevent him from seeking its repetition. From me in this meaning as well:

*You keep following one glance with another,*
*after every beautiful woman and beautiful man.*

*You think that this is the cure for your wound, but in reality*
*it is a wound upon a wound.*

*You slaughtered your gaze with glances and weeping,*
*so the heart is slaughtered by you, what a slaughter!*

It has been said: "Restraining the glances is easier than enduring the lasting regrets."

**The Passing Thought**

As for passing thoughts, their matter is more difficult, for they are the origin of good and evil. From them are generated resolves, aspirations and determinations. Whoever observes his passing thoughts takes the reins of his soul and subdues his desire. Whoever is overcome by his passing thoughts, his desire and soul will overpower him. Whoever takes passing thoughts lightly will be dragged by force into destruction. Passing thoughts keep recurring upon the heart until they become vain wishes.

﴿Like a mirage in a level plain, which the thirsty one thinks is water; until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing, and finds Allah with him, who pays him his account in full. And Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾ [al-Nur: 39]

The lowest of people in aspiration and the most debased in soul is the one who is content from realities with false hopes, who draws them to himself and is pleased by them. By the life of Allah, these are the capital of the bankrupt, the merchandise of the idle, and the food of the empty soul, which has settled for union through a phantom visit of imagination, and for realities through deceptive hopes. As the poet said:

*Hopes from Su'da, a refreshment for the thirsty:*
*Su'da gave us them, cold, when we were parched.*

*Wishes, if they are real, they are the finest wishes;*
*and if not, we have lived in them a time of ease.*

They are the most harmful thing to a person. From them come incapacity and laziness, and they produce neglect, regret and remorse. The one who wishes, when the reality itself escapes him physically, transforms its image in his heart, embraces it and presses it to himself, and is content with union with an imagined, illusory image that his thinking has shaped.

This does not benefit him at all. His case is like that of the hungry and the thirsty who picture in their minds the image of food and drink, while they neither eat nor drink.

Settling into this and seeking it out indicates the soul's loss and baseness. The honor and purity of the soul, its elevation, lie in negating from it every passing thought that has no reality, refusing to let it occur to the mind, and feeling disdain for himself at it.

Then the passing thoughts are divided into categories that revolve around four principles:

Passing thoughts by which the servant draws the benefits of his worldly life.
Passing thoughts by which he repels the harms of his worldly life.
Passing thoughts by which he draws the benefits of his afterlife.
Passing thoughts by which he repels the harms of his afterlife.

So the servant should confine his passing thoughts, reflections and concerns to these four categories. When they are confined to these, it becomes possible for him to gather them and not leave them to others. When passing thoughts crowd upon him because their objects are crowded, he should give priority to the more important and then the next most important, the one he fears losing, and delay the one that is less important and that he does not fear losing.

(Two other categories remain.)

One is important and will not be lost.
The other is not important but will be lost.

In each of these there is something calling for giving it priority, so here hesitation and bewilderment occur. If he gives priority to the important, he fears losing what is lesser; if he gives priority to what is lesser, he loses occupation with the important. Likewise, two matters may present themselves that cannot be combined, and neither can be obtained except by losing the other.

This is the place where intellect, understanding and knowledge are put to use. From here some rise and some succeed, and others fail. Most of those whose intellect and knowledge are great prefer the unimportant that will not be lost over the important that will be lost. You will not find anyone who is safe from this, but some are more and some less.

Judgment in this matter rests on the supreme principle upon which the Sharia and the divine decree depend, and to which the creation and the command return: preferring the greater of two benefits and the higher of them, even if the lesser benefit is lost, and entering the lesser of two harms to repel what is greater.

So one forfeits a benefit to attain what is greater than it, and commits a harm to repel what is greater than it.

Thus the thoughts and reflections of the intelligent person do not exceed this, and it is for this that the Sharias came, and the benefits of this world and the next can only stand upon this. The highest, most sublime and most beneficial of thoughts is what is for Allah and the Last Abode. What is for Allah is of several kinds:

The first is reflection upon His revealed verses, understanding them, grasping their meaning and what He intends by them. For this reason Allah the Exalted sent them down, not merely for their recitation, but recitation is a means.

Some of the early generation (*salaf*) said: "The Qur'an was sent down to be acted upon, so they took its recitation as the action."

The second is reflection upon His visible signs, taking lessons from them, and using them as evidence for His names and attributes, His wisdom, His beneficence, His kindness and His generosity. Allah, glorified is He, urged His servants to reflect upon His signs, to ponder them and comprehend them, and He censured the one heedless of this.

The third is reflection upon His blessings and His beneficence, and His bounty upon His creation with all kinds of favors, and the vastness of His mercy, His forgiveness and His forbearance.

These three kinds draw out from the heart knowledge of Allah, love of Him, fear of Him and hope in Him. Constant reflection on this, together with remembrance, dyes the heart completely in knowledge and love.

The fourth is reflection upon the faults and diseases of the soul, and the faults of deeds. This reflection is of great benefit, and it is the gate to every good. Its effect is in breaking the commanding soul that enjoins evil. When it is broken, the tranquil soul lives and rises, and rule belongs to it, so the heart is revived, its word circulates in its kingdom, and it dispatches its commanders and soldiers for its interests.

The fifth is reflection upon the duty of the present time and its task, and gathering all one's concern upon it. The one who knows the value of the moment is the son of his time. If he wastes it, all his interests are lost, for all interests arise from the time. If he squanders it, he will never recover it.

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I accompanied the Sufis and gained from them only two words: one of them is their saying, 'Time is a sword; if you do not cut it, it will cut you.'"

He mentioned the other phrase: "And if you do not occupy your soul with the truth, it will occupy you with falsehood."

A person's time is in reality his life. It is the material of his eternal life in everlasting bliss, and the material of a narrow living in painful punishment. It passes faster than clouds. What is of his time for Allah and with Allah is his true life and lifespan. Anything other than that is not counted from his life, and if he lives through it, he lives the life of beasts. When he spends his time in heedlessness, forgetfulness and vain hopes, and the best way he passes it is sleep and idleness, then the death of such a person is better for him than his life.

And if the servant, even while in prayer, has from his prayer only what he understood of it, then he has from his lifespan only what was in it with Allah and for Allah.

As for what is outside these categories of passing thoughts and reflections, it is either satanic whisperings, or vain wishes and false deceptions, like the thoughts of those afflicted in their minds: the drunk, the bewildered and the obsessive. The tongue of the state of these people says at the unveiling of realities:

*If my station with You on the Gathering is what I have met,*
*then I have wasted my days.*

*A wish my soul clung to for a time,*
*and today I reckon it as jumbled dreams.*

Know that the arrival of a passing thought does no harm; what harms is summoning it and conversing with it. The passing thought is like a passer-by on the road: if you leave it, it passes by and goes away from you; if you invite it, it bewitches you with its talk and its deceit. It is the lightest thing for the empty, vain soul, and the heaviest thing for the heart and the noble, heavenly, tranquil soul.

Allah, glorified is He, has composed in man two souls: a commanding soul and a tranquil soul. They are hostile to each other. Whatever is light for one is heavy for the other, and whatever the one enjoys, the other suffers from. For the commanding soul there is nothing harder than acting for Allah and preferring His pleasure over its desire, and there is nothing more beneficial to it than that. And for the tranquil soul there is nothing harder than acting for other than Allah, and what the caller of desire brings.
